effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices, agroforestry trees and shrubs add habitat and species diversity relative to the land uses they replace. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system had the largest earthworm Simpson diversity index (0.62) against the smallest in sole pigeon pea (0.41) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry than in monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a coffee meta-analysis found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems than conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Niger, FMNR adoption increased tree diversity by one to three tree species per farm [ev_biodiversity_outcome_haglund11_1], and a WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates both animal diversity and habitat diversity increased, noting many animal species find safe habitats in new FMNR sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_507_2019_habitat_diversity]. In Colombian silvopasture, a global meta-analysis found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with the gain largest for invertebrates (53.7%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]; a Colombian World Bank project evaluation reports increased species richness and abundance, including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8], bird monitoring there found four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. For linear plantings, reviews state that windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2], that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation across fragmented tropical farm landscapes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4], and that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. Farmers in Colombia and Costa Rica report that live fences increase landscape connectivity, creating local corridors for fauna and flora, which they see as positive for native biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. A tropical agroforestry meta-analysis found natural enemies of pests significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A global silvopastoral meta-analysis breaks the 28.4% biodiversity gain down further: native-tree silvopasture held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and planted-tree silvopasture held 20.9% more, with invertebrate abundance specifically about 60% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2]. In Maradi's Dan Saga and Aguié villages in Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration took local woody species richness from only a few types of tree in the 1980s to at least 30 tree species today, with farmers reintroducing species that had disappeared [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_4].
conditionality: The roll-up reads strong because its strongest-evidenced sub-practices do: silvopastoral, shaded perennial-crop and planted silvoarable systems each read a strong gain on their own, and none of the remaining sub-practices (cross-family, linear-boundary, regeneration-based farmland, each reading only a slight gain) is large or negative enough to pull the pooled picture down or flip the direction. Set against the gains, when traditional shaded coffee/cacao agroforest is intensified to sparse-shade plantation, a global meta-analysis found total species richness fell 46% and forest-species richness fell 65%, and converting natural forest to agroforest itself cost 11% of total species richness and 35% of forest-species richness — measured harm from two independent sources, read against intensification and against standing forest rather than against open farmland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1 t/ha were not attainable with more than 10 associated tree species, a direct yield-biodiversity trade-off [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The same silvopastoral meta-analysis that found a gain against open pasture also found native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower biodiversity than native forest — a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture counterfactual, so it does not contradict the open-pasture gain [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. A windbreak study in Queensland found the plantings useful for some birds but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, with much lower wildlife value than riparian vegetation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3], and the same pest-control meta-analysis that found more natural enemies found no significant effect of agroforestry on natural-enemy diversity in most studies (7 of 11) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. Most units describe direction without a size, and the meta-analyses behind the clearest numbers (cocoa intensification, silvopasture) do not enumerate their study countries, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1]. A review of the same kind of Mexican coffee intensification gradient found species richness of ants, butterflies and birds declining as shade is simplified from forest through traditional and commercial polyculture to shaded monoculture, echoing the intensification harm already in this row [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1]. A nature-based-solutions policy review frames the biodiversity benefit as likely but conditional: it depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species planted, not a guaranteed property of agroforestry as such [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3]. The new Colombian dung-beetle evidence adds a fourth independent silvopastoral source and reads as a benefit, reinforcing rather than offsetting the measured harm already in this row [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2]. The gain is also not guaranteed by the practice alone: a Sahelian synthesis notes this is not always the case, since in some regions farmers protect Faidherbia albida with priority over other species, producing something closer to a monoculture than a diverse parkland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_boton10_5].

effect_mechanism: On pastoral rangeland, trees raise biodiversity mainly by adding habitat structure and by supporting seed dispersal into the pasture. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral systems (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found biodiversity 28.4% higher in silvopasture than in open pastures; broken down by system type, silvopasture built around existing native trees held 36.3% more biodiversity than open pasture and silvopasture with planted trees held 20.9% more, with invertebrate biodiversity specifically 53.7% higher under native-tree silvopasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Costa Rican cattle pastures, a review of Central American silvopastoral research reports that windbreak trees support seed rain — animals visiting the trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the landscape — and cites a study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4].

effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices pooled together, agroforestry trees and shrubs are reported to add habitat and pest-control value. A tropical-agroforestry review states that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation, and that retaining or establishing trees in agricultural land may be a critical component of conservation efforts in fragmented landscapes, with floristic diversity that can be high and a substantial number of animal species able to exploit these habitats for feeding, movement and, in some cases, reproduction [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. conditionality: The same meta-analysis that found more natural enemies also reports, for the diversity (rather than abundance) of natural enemies, that most studies (7 of 11) showed no effect and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect and the rest split evenly between positive and negative — held out here as a finding on a narrower measure of the same taxon group, not a contradiction of the abundance result [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. effect_mechanism: Linear plantings add woody habitat structure to farmland. A tropical-agroforestry review states that, depending on their floristic diversity, structural complexity and management, windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species, including a limited number of forest-dependent species, by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2]. A review of silvopastoral research in Central America adds that animals visiting windbreak trees carry and deposit tree seeds, letting woody species persist and potentially re-establish in the pasture landscape, and cites a Costa Rican study finding significantly greater seed-rain density and species richness in windbreaks than in open pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_dagang03_4]. In Colombia and Costa Rica, farmers report that planting live fences increases landscape connectivity, creating local corridors that both fauna and flora can use, which they see as positive for native biodiversity conservation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. The same review also reports a mixed case: in Queensland, Australia, planted eucalyptus windbreaks were useful habitat for some bird species but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, and held much lower value as wildlife habitat than riparian vegetation, which the authors attribute to the windbreaks' lower structural complexity and single-species planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].
conditionality: The class stays slight because one of the three units finds no added value for mammals and forest specialists relative to riparian habitat, holding agreement at medium rather than high [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3]. None of the three states a size for the conservation gain: the windbreak review is a generalisation across cited temperate studies, the live-fence unit is a farmer-perception survey across Colombia and Costa Rica (upper-middle and high income), and neither names the countries, income group or farming system behind the pooled row, which is why confidence stays low and the row only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].

effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cacao systems, more structurally complex agroforestry supports more species than simpler, intensified alternatives. A ten-country cocoa meta-analysis found cocoa agroforestry held a significantly higher number of animal species, pooled across taxa, than cocoa monoculture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. A review of shaded coffee systems found bird diversity 120 to 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems of varying complexity than in conventional coffee [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. Comparing coffee/cacao agroforest against a more intensified sparse-shade plantation, a response-ratio study found total species richness and forest-species richness both significantly higher under agroforest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. Along a Mexican coffee-intensification gradient (forest, traditional polyculture, commercial polyculture, shaded monoculture), estimated ant, butterfly and bird richness was higher at the less-intensified, more complex-shade end of the gradient that agroforestry occupies [ev_biodiversity_outcome_perf05_1].

effect_mechanism: In Colombian silvopastoral systems, biodiversity rises relative to open pasture, the land use the practice replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Invertebrate abundance showed the largest taxon-specific gain against open pasture, 53.7% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Colombia specifically, a World Bank project evaluation reports that silvopastoral systems played a major role in increasing and conserving biodiversity at farm and landscape level, raising the number of species (richness) and individuals observed (abundance), including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; bird monitoring on Colombian cattle farms found intensive silvopasture had four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A tropical-agroforestry review states that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. A further Colombian Andes study of dung beetles — an indicator of ecological-process recovery, not just species counts — found significantly more beetles caught per trap in intensive silvopasture than in the treeless improved pasture it replaced (275 individuals across five species against 143 across three species), with the same three species found in both land uses plus two additional species recorded only in the silvopastoral system [ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_giraldo10_2].
conditionality: The same global meta-analysis measures silvopasture against a second, different benchmark — ungrazed native forest — and there the sign reverses: native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower overall biodiversity, 14.8% lower plant biodiversity and 24.4% lower invertebrate biodiversity than native forest, with invertebrate abundance 30.2% lower [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_9, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_11]. This is a conservation benchmark, not the intervention counterfactual: it means silvopasture holds less biodiversity than intact forest, not that converting grazing land to silvopasture reduces biodiversity, so the class is set from the open-pasture comparisons and these forest-benchmark units are held out of it. Two further forest-benchmark comparisons, for birds and bird species richness, found no significant difference, and the invertebrate-abundance gain against open pasture was itself not significant despite a large point estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The meta-analysis does not report the countries behind its figures, so only the Colombian project evidence anchors this row to the LIC/LMIC target; as a pooled global figure it transfers only as adjacent [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The bird-diversity review's single worked example compares recently abandoned pasture against actively grazed pasture, so grazing cessation is confounded with the trees themselves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1]. These two new dung-beetle units read as a benefit and are weighted heavily enough, alongside the existing Colombian evidence, to move this row's own class from a moderate to a strong gain; they do not touch the separate forest-benchmark comparisons already held out of the class above.

effect_mechanism: Trees on farmland add a carbon store that cropland or pasture without trees lacks: carbon builds up in trunks, branches and roots above and below ground, and leaf litter and root turnover raise soil organic carbon over time. Field measurements illustrate the range: agroforestry systems in East Africa were found to store an average of 24.2 Mg of carbon per hectare in biomass and 98.8 Mg per hectare in the soil, tree-based systems pooled across tropical, arid, temperate and boreal sites stored an average of 46.1 Mg C/ha in biomass, and in Ghana, cocoa grown at the recommended density of shade trees achieved a 127% greater greenhouse-gas removal increment than cocoa grown in full sun.
conditionality: The pooled evidence leans heavily on global and cited modelled assessments (including IPCC chapters) rather than new field measurement, so the class is capped at a moderate level even though field studies and the IPCC syntheses point the same way. A few field trials (in the Sahel, and in pantropical cocoa systems) found no statistically significant difference in soil carbon or soil chemistry between agroforestry and the comparison land use, and net greenhouse-gas effects (including methane and nitrous oxide) were inconsistent in some pantropical site comparisons.

effect_mechanism: In tree-perennial systems such as shade coffee, more and more diverse shade trees store more carbon. In Nicaragua, carbon stored ranged from 7.8 Mg per hectare in unshaded coffee to 35.3 Mg per hectare in coffee with the most diversified shade, with the woody shade trees holding 74% of that carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_pinoar14_1]. In the same region, traditional shaded-coffee polyculture held a mean above-ground tree carbon stock of 41 t per hectare, against 16 t per hectare in a more simplified commercial polyculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_rahn14_1]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis of cocoa systems found 2.5 times more biomass carbon stored in agroforestry than in full-sun monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1].
conditionality: The same pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found no significant difference in soil organic carbon or other soil chemical properties between agroforestry and monoculture, so the carbon gain in this family sits mainly in the trees' own biomass rather than the soil [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]. The Nicaraguan figures are for shaded coffee specifically, and the size of the gain depends on how much shade-tree diversity and density the system carries.

effect_mechanism: Pooled across sub-practices, modelled mitigation-potential and stock-comparison studies consistently find a carbon benefit, though almost none of them gives a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. effect_mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. In the Colombian Amazon (Caquetá), a chronosequence comparing silvopasture against the traditional pasture it replaced found no significant change in total soil organic carbon stock over the full sampled soil profile, but did find a gain confined to the deepest sampled layer, read by the authors as a sign the practice could turn the soil into a carbon sink in deeper layers over time [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_2]. A review of pastures in semi-arid north-eastern Brazil reports a similar pattern: retaining native tree species (Ziziphus joazeiro and Spondias tuberosa) in pasture significantly raised total soil carbon compared with open pasture away from the trees, attributed to litterfall and fine-root turnover adding soil organic matter and to nitrogen fixation, though the review gives no carbon value [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].
conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. All of this is global meta-analysis evidence without a Colombia/Costa Rica-specific breakdown, so only the World Bank project and Costa Rican figures anchor the row to its stated countries; as pooled global findings the SOC units transfer only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. Two further readings from the same Colombian Amazon chronosequence measure silvopasture's shallow surface-layer soil carbon against standing native forest rather than against the pasture it replaced, with the traditional pasture on the same land showing a comparable or larger gain over forest in that layer; the engine holds these out of the class for the same reason as the earlier forest-benchmark comparisons in this row — they measure recovery toward a forest reference, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual, and here the gain mostly reflects grass-root carbon inputs after conversion rather than the trees [ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_olaya20_4]. The full-profile null and the unstated-size deeper-layer gain both count toward the same-direction pool without stating a size, which is why only a minority of the same-direction units in this row state how big the effect is, holding the class at moderate; the system is also bundled with tillage, lime and phosphate-rock application at establishment, so the gain cannot be credited to the trees alone. The Brazilian pasture finding is a narrative review citing an underlying primary study without giving its own carbon value or stating the study's duration, so it corroborates the direction of the SOC gain without adding a size [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dagang03_1].

A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. In Niger, during the 2005 food crisis, farmers practising farmer-managed natural regeneration were less severely affected than other farmers and recorded relatively lower infant mortality, through income from selling wood and other forest products [ev_food_security_boton10_2].

effect_mechanism: IPCC assessments link agroforestry to food security through diversification of production that avoids trade-offs between crop and tree products, and an East African systematic review finds that the fodder, food, firewood and income from agroforestry act as safety nets in climate shocks [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7, ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. The IPCC land report estimates that up to 1.3 billion people on degrading land could benefit in food security through agroforestry [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. Under Regreening Africa the share of respondents consuming at least five of the ten food items rose from 16 to 21, a 31 percent increase, and households that intensified their use of tree products saw significant gains in dietary diversity [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. In the Nepal mid-hills the share of food-sufficient households rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry project [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Nyando, Kenya, agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies in hunger periods and some relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Rwanda tree density was associated with higher food security in some agroecologies [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. A global review of nature-based solutions for food security cites population-survey studies finding better food access where agroforestry was applied in southern Africa, Brazil and China over periods of up to 20 years [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. A systematic review of agroforestry adoption in sub-Saharan Africa, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, finds that agroforestry recurrently enhances dietary diversity, particularly where fruit- and vegetable-producing trees are included [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food throughout the year for 40% of households against 18% of households using traditional practices [ev_food_security_reyes05_1].
conditionality: Few units say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate. In Rwanda's Buberuka Highlands more trees went with lower food security, a measured harm, while in Congo Nile the association ran the other way [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Regreening Africa FIES score showed no substantial change, moving from 4.9 to 4.8, and the Campbell systematic review found the impact on nutrition and food security beneficial or neutral across the studies it covered [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9, ev_food_security_castle21s_4]. The Regreening Africa and Nepal results are before-and-after surveys with no control group, and the Nepal project bundled the trees with market linkage, training, subsidies and organic fertiliser [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, so part of the food-sufficiency gap is a livestock and wealth effect [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan review notes that outcomes vary with agroforestry type, complementary practices and the wider context, and gives no pooled food-security estimate [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. The IPCC figure is a count of people who could benefit, not a measured effect [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. The food-access review included only studies showing improvement in at least one food-security dimension, so its finding says nothing about studies that found no benefit, and one of its cited studies is a life-cycle assessment rather than a population survey [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. effect_mechanism: Shade from trees and shelterbelts lowers air and soil temperature, reducing heat stress for crops and livestock across many systems. Oil-palm alley cropping with black pepper or cacao in Malaysia cooled air by 1.3 degrees Celsius and soil surface by 2.1 degrees Celsius compared with a 15-year oil-palm monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_3]; silvopastoral arrangements in Colombia and Costa Rica cooled paddocks by 1.7 to 3.6 degrees Celsius relative to open pasture, with tree groups giving the largest effect [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]; shelterbelts in China significantly lowered summer air temperature by 4.01% and raised relative humidity by 13.45% [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]; and under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature fell by up to 6 degrees Celsius, with the open field reaching 36 degrees Celsius against 29 degrees Celsius under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A systematic review of silvopastoral studies found silvopastoral systems were mostly (57%) measured as having lower air temperature, soil-surface temperature and radiant heat load than treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1].
conditionality: The same shade can also warm conditions or show no significant effect, depending on species, age and season. In the Malaysian oil-palm trial, alleys intercropped with bamboo or bactris palm were significantly hotter (up to 37.0 degrees Celsius air temperature) than the monocultures, and the authors judged these two species unsuitable intercrops because of the increased air temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_ashraf19_4]. A Mexican coffee shade-gradient study found no significant difference in mean air temperature between high- and low-shade sites in either the wet or dry season, even though the high-shade site fluctuated less around the optimum temperature [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. In Senegal, windbreak hedges were reported to generally cause a slight rise in temperature in protected plots rather than cooling, with effects varying by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. In the systematic review of silvopastoral systems, four of the seven cattle studies using the temperature-humidity index found no significant difference between silvopastoral and treeless pasture, partly because that index does not capture solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees reduce heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. Most of the quantified cooling is measured in upper-middle- and high-income countries (Malaysia, Brazil, Germany, China); evidence from low-income parkland systems in Ethiopia and the Sahel is present but thinner.

effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping, trees and shelterbelts cool the crop. Under Faidherbia albida parkland trees in Ethiopia, midday air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C against the open field, peaking at 29oC under the canopy versus 36oC outside [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland found shelterbelts reduced summer air temperature by 4.01% against unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1], and a review reports, second-hand, that poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. In semi-arid Kenya, dispersed Grevillea robusta trees over maize lowered the maize's own seasonal mean maximum growing-point temperature by 2.5 to 6.0 degrees C compared with unshaded sole maize, depending on the season [ev_microclimate_buffering_lott09_5].
conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: an FAO review in Senegal states, second-hand, that windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots, with impacts varying by crop and growth stage, so shelter designs that cut wind may warm rather than cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The units measure air temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not heat-stress yield losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. They span low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Senegal, upper-middle-income China and high-income Germany [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. That Kenyan cooling was measured on a dispersed-tree system that also cut maize grain yield severely in the same seasons, so the cooler microclimate did not translate into a production benefit there [ev_microclimate_buffering_lott09_5].

effect_mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
conditionality: The Colombian and Brazilian review results are cited secondary findings from upper-middle-income settings, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. All units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

effect_mechanism: Agroforestry's effect on the crop-yield gap depends heavily on how close the trees stand to the crop. In a global review of windbreak and alley systems, wider tree spacing lifted yield — modelling predicted an 8.04% yield gain over a 20 tree-height buffer for windbreaks, and a 13% gain at 15 tree-heights for alley systems [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8]. The same review found the opposite at close spacing: alleys under 10 tree-heights had reduced yields, and those under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. In dryland agriculture, a separate literature review reported agroforestry techniques raising cereal yields by 69% on average [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14].
conditionality: At the whole-agroforestry level the sub-practices disagree with one another, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than picking a side: alley/boundary tree systems and shaded-perennial systems split between gain and loss by spacing and shade design, while regeneration-based systems point positive. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 39 sources. A livestock-yield check on linear agroforestry, drawn from only 12 publications covering 36 paddock-years, could not establish an effect in either direction [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13]. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2]. effect_mechanism: In high-income, often mechanised cropping systems, trees compete with the adjacent crop for light, water and nutrients. Canadian Prairie shelterbelt studies found a competition zone of reduced crop yield close to the trees and a wind-sheltered zone further out with above-average yields, but the net effect across the field was often a loss — one study estimated a net yield loss equivalent to the width of the shelterbelt. Pea yields under trees fell by 25% to 77% depending on rainfall regime, and a Brazilian shaded-coffee comparison found a 30% yield reduction in the shaded system relative to monoculture.
conditionality: The direction is not uniform even within high-income systems: several Costa Rican shaded-coffee comparisons found no significant yield difference against full sun, and non-grain or livestock components improved under trees even as grain and legume yields fell — tuber and bean yields rose at a subarctic Ontario site, and cattle weight gains and milk yield were reported higher under trees in Costa Rica. The negative result is strongest for annual grain and legume intercrops competing directly with tree roots and shade, not for every component of these farming systems.

effect_mechanism: Among low- and lower-middle-income contexts, agroforestry's yield effect is positive on average but varies sharply by sub-practice. Pooled across studies, the standardized effect on crop yield was +1.16 (Hedges' g), with a 95% confidence interval of −0.35 to 2.67 [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]; a single Malawi study of fertiliser-tree fallows rotated with maize found a much larger effect of 3.85 on crop value, used as a proxy for yield [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3]. In the shrub- and tree-parklands of Sudano-Sahelian West Africa, millet and sorghum yields ranged from 25% lower to 120% higher where shrubs grew in the fields, and were even more variable — 100% lower to 200% higher — where trees rather than shrubs were present [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2]. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7].
conditionality: The gains are not universal: a hedgerow-intercropping subgroup in a sub-Saharan Africa review found a crop-yield response ratio of only 0.9 (95% CI 0.9 to 1.0), spanning the no-effect value of 1 — the one configuration in that dataset where agroforestry did not lift yield [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; and a payment-for-ecosystem-services tree-planting programme showed an effect as low as −0.33 (Hedges' g) at the low end of the same review's range [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 18 sources. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2].

effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light. Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. In canal-irrigated Haryana, India, a Eucalyptus biodrainage planting along field boundaries lowered the water table and raised wheat grain yield 3.4 times over compared with adjacent waterlogged fields without the plantation, though near the tree lines shading and root competition cut wheat yield by an estimated 11.7% [ev_crop_yield_ram11_2, ev_crop_yield_ram11_3].

effect_mechanism: Across silvopastoral systems, tree cover consistently raises forage and livestock output relative to open pasture. In Senegal, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies reached 2 to 5 times that measured in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Reviews report tree shade in pastures associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain generally [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4], and in Nicaragua and Costa Rica, milk production was 29% and over 15% higher on high tree-density or silvopasture compared with low-cover or full-sun pasture, with dry-season liveweight gains 2 to 5% higher on high-tree-density pasture, attributed to lower heat stress and more available foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In Colombia, intensive silvopasture raised milk production 32.1% over the same pasture grasses without shrubs or trees, raised milk per hectare per year under Leucaena against an open-field system, and a review reports beef output 12-fold higher per unit of land than traditional grazing, also higher than improved treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture is also reported to raise stocking rate several-fold over extensive grazing, with proportional gains in meat and milk output, and better cattle feeding in critical drought periods is said to reduce seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During a severe drought, Colombian silvopastoral forage production held steady while grass-monoculture biomass fell to a quarter, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are described as more drought-tolerant, giving more stable dry-season forage volumes [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. A review also reports that integrating a grazed fodder bank — fodder trees or shrubs established on part of the pasture and then grazed — repeatedly raises animal production, though the gain is delayed by the trees' establishment period and by taking part of the pasture out of use while they establish [ev_livestock_productivity_dagang03_5]. In arid India, trees and shrubs lopped for green leaf fodder supply sheep, goats and camels with browse in drought years, when grass is scarce [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].
conditionality: Gains are not universal. Under high-density Acacia decurrens silvopasture in Colombia, milk per cow per day was lower than in the open field, though a lower-density silvopasture at the same site still out-performed the open field, showing tree density itself can flip the sign [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. A review of Brazilian silvopastoral thermal-comfort and production studies found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. During El Niño events, silvopastoral systems in Colombia still lost milk production, just less than conventional systems did [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. The Argentine multi-site forage evidence is the clearest statement that the benefit is severity- and site-dependent: it held in humid areas in both normal and dry years, showed no difference in semi-arid areas, and reversed from a slight gain to an 89% loss in a dry year at one semi-arid site, with denser canopy generally associated with lower relative forage production across sites [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_3, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_4, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. Most of the Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume rather than new primary measurements, and the clearest primary magnitudes (Colombia, Nicaragua, Costa Rica) are upper-middle or high income, while the Senegalese fodder evidence is lower-middle income, which is why this row's evidence sits adjacent to, rather than squarely inside, the LIC/LMIC target. Against this, a review of a regional silvopastoral conservation project in Esparza, Costa Rica reports that unpruned multistrata live fences can reduce forage availability by shading out the grasses along pasture edges [ev_forage_productivity_garbach12_1]. The same arid-India trial that supplies the browse-fodder finding also measured lower understorey herbage yield under every tree and shrub species than in a treeless control during drought years, a trade-off between the forage layers that this row's gain does not net off [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2].

effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of agroforestry adoption by smallholders in sub-Saharan Africa found a significant yield gain for maize in the high-quality studies (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42), and a pan-tropical meta-analysis of pest control reports that the only studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found a gain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2, ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1].
conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, the sub-Saharan adoption meta-analysis found that agroforestry overall is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1], an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. effect_mechanism: Planted silvoarable systems — trees planted in rows with crops growing between them — show genuinely opposite results depending on spacing and tree type, not simply weak evidence. In a global review, wide alley spacing raised yield (13% at 15 tree-heights) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8], while the same review's overall average across 333 individual paddock-years was a 17.63% yield loss, with only 69 of those 333 responses (21%) showing a gain [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6]; narrower alleys under 2.5 tree-heights lost more than 25% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7]. Pulling the other way, a Malawi study of fertiliser-tree fallows rotated with maize raised crop value by 3.85 (Hedges' g) [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3], and a sub-Saharan Africa review found alley cropping lifting the crop-yield response ratio to 2.1 against the non-agroforestry control [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_3].
conditionality: The class is left as conflicting evidence rather than a pooled average because both sides carry real weight: a Kenyan biomass-transfer trial found a yield effect so large the authors called it "extraordinarily high... beyond reasonable effects based on nutrient content of the biomass", while an improved-fallow trial in the same study was not statistically significant [ev_crop_yield_place05_6]. Measured harm (maladaptation) — the practice reducing production for some adopters — appears in 14 sources within this family. A Kenyan on-station alley-cropping trial in Embu adds a direct species contrast within one experiment: maize alley-cropped with leucaena yielded significantly more than both the unfertilised and fertilised maize-monoculture controls, while the same maize alley-cropped with calliandra yielded less than the unfertilised control — same site, same design, opposite signs by hedgerow species [ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_1, ev_crop_yield_mugendi99_2].

effect_mechanism: Regeneration-based agroforestry (farmer-managed natural regeneration and similar on-farm tree regrowth) raises farm productivity mainly through soil-fertility gains under scattered trees and diversified tree products, not necessarily through higher grain yield directly beneath the trees — in Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration did not significantly increase grain yields, with the added value instead coming from higher yields of other crops such as cowpea. In Niger, millet yields on fields with regenerated trees (100 to 370 kg/ha) were higher than on control fields without trees (50 to 270 kg/ha), a gain of 50 to 100 kg/ha the authors attribute to tree presence, and the same protected trees supply dry-season fodder that eases the feed shortage common at that time of year [ev_crop_yield_boton10_1, ev_forage_productivity_boton10_7].
conditionality: Two sources measured harm: cereal yield reductions have been observed under specific tree species in the Sahel, and groundnut yields fell under one native tree's canopy. Effects vary strongly by tree species and distance from the trunk — some species are associated with cereal yield gains, others with losses — and a modelled Ethiopian trial found wheat yield did not respond to temperature change without added nitrogen, so the benefit depends on fertility management as much as on regeneration itself.

effect_mechanism: Trees in a pasture add shade, deep-rooted drought buffering and nitrogen transfer to the grass layer, but they also compete with pasture grasses for light, water and nutrients; which effect wins depends on tree density and age. A global meta-analysis of silvopastoral paddocks found pasture yield fell by an average of 20.8% across 345 paddock-years and by 30% once tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, while newly planted trees had no effect at all and the oldest trees reduced pasture yield to below 50% of the open-pasture control [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_11, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12]. Livestock yield across the same global dataset fell by 18.6% on average, but 33% of paddock-years still showed higher animal productivity under trees than in the open [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14], and the decline levelled off once density passed about 300 trees per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15]. Nitrogen-fixing trees can also transfer nitrogen to companion grasses: Setaria grass grown with leucaena in Sri Lanka had a 16% higher nitrogen yield than a grass monoculture [ev_forage_productivity_dagang03_2].
conditionality: The sign flips with drought severity and site. Pooled across Argentine sites, silvopastoral forage production exceeded treeless grassland in both normal and dry years where the dry year's rainfall shortfall stayed at or below 35% of the long-term mean, but reversed into a competition process once the shortfall exceeded 35% [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_1, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_2]. At one site the silvopastoral relative response went from +2% in normal years to -89% in a dry year, while at another site with a smaller shortfall the response went the opposite way, from -15% in normal years to +26% in the dry year [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_5, ev_forage_productivity_peri24_6]. The same study found forage production fell further as tree cover (shade intensity) increased, in both normal and dry years [ev_forage_productivity_peri24_7]. In arid India, herbage yield under most tree and shrub species was lower than the treeless control during drought years, significantly so for Acacia tortilis and Dichrostachys nutans, but the trees also produced leaf fodder that households cut for livestock during the same droughts, a trade-off of less grass for more browse [ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_1, ev_forage_productivity_singhrao08_2]. In New Zealand radiata-pine silvopasture, early complementarity between trees and pasture reversed as the trees matured, and by 15 years after planting the pasture had disappeared entirely under the trees [ev_forage_productivity_pollock08_1]. In a US silvopasture trial, forage was significantly lower under trees than in open pasture a year after establishment [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_1], though the difference was no longer significant in the second year, with the authors citing the small sample size [ev_forage_productivity_orefice16_2]. At the high-intensity end, an intensive Colombian silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows per hectare and milk production to 130% of the conventional baseline while eliminating chemical fertiliser, and kept forage production constant through intense drought when a grass monoculture lost 25% of its biomass [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Most of the quantified evidence is from upper-middle- and high-income countries (Argentina, the United States, New Zealand); the arid-India and Sri Lanka units are the main lower-middle-income evidence.

effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage study by Ram et al. found a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, well above the 1.3:1 the same authors report for ordinary agricultural crops in Haryana, with returns from selling the trees after only an initial planting and maintenance cost [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese figure is an earlier study read second-hand in a review [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. The Indian figure now comes from the original Ram et al. study rather than a second-hand reading, but it is still a single planting's first-rotation harvest, not a repeated or ongoing return [ev_economic_return_ram11_4]. The Chinese trial covers only the establishment years, and in the same trial the intercropped soybean and alfalfa yielded much less than sole crops, so the cash-flow gain comes from the fruit trees rather than from the crop [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The evidence comes from lower-middle-income Senegal and India and upper-middle-income China.

effect_mechanism: In pastoral rangeland systems, silvopastoral conversion mostly pays once established. In Peru and Colombia, an intensive silvopastoral system had an operating benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1]. In the Colombian Amazon, producer income from milk sales rose 42.12 percent under an intensive silvopastoral system owing to its higher carrying capacity of 2.71 against 1.84 animal units for the intensive system and grass monoculture respectively [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1]. In Nicaragua, a modelled 20-hectare beef and dairy farm found silvopastoral net income overtaking traditional pasture income only in the fifth year after establishment [ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].
conditionality: Against this, in Brazil a review of barriers to silvopastoral adoption states that, for this reason, farm income in the first years after establishing a silvopastoral system would be comparatively lower than under traditional pasture [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1]. The Brazilian and Nicaraguan units are an expert review and a modelled single-farm case rather than measured trials, the Peru-Colombia benefit-cost ratio is cited within a systematic review, and the milk-income gain already carries the cattle-stocking change that drives it, so the finding is reported as an establishment-phase income dip followed by a payback once the system matures [ev_economic_return_diasf08_1, ev_economic_return_diasf08_2].

effect_mechanism: Planted silvoarable systems, trees grown in rows with arable crops, raise income mainly through fertiliser-tree soil fertility effects, intercrop diversification, and eventual timber or fruit harvests on top of the annual crop. Net revenue from a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea intercrop in India was reported as up to 2.66 times higher than the pigeon pea sole crop [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1], and alley cropping with Acacia senegal in Sudan raised sorghum net revenue from 501 to 558 Sudanese pounds per hectare [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4]. Eucalyptus timber intercropped with field crops in India gave a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5 to 1, compared with 1.3 to 1 for agricultural crops alone [ev_economic_return_ram11_4], and alley cropping in Nigeria returned a net present value of 1755 Nigerian naira per hectare, more than the no-till and other alley-cropping comparators [ev_economic_return_ehui90_7]. Fertiliser trees also protect farmers against drought-year crop failure: in Zambia, a farmer who had planted fertiliser trees lost only 90 US dollars in sunk cost when a crop failed, against 164 US dollars for a farmer who had invested in inorganic fertiliser [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1].
conditionality: The benefit depends on which intercrop combination and management regime is used, and is not universal. A meta-analysis found that crop-fruit tree intercropping in China had a negative effect on productivity [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and the same Indian Gmelina trial's higher net returns were measured against a high-cost mango sole crop, so the size of the gain depends on the alternative crop chosen [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. In Nigeria, net present value for sweet orange monocropped or intercropped was negative for the monocrop and for one intercrop combination, and positive only with cassava and maize or with chilli pepper and amaranthus [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Alley cropping with nitrogen-fixing trees and mulch from multi-purpose trees was profitable in land- and labour-abundant conditions [ev_economic_return_korm99_5] but, as the same source separately records, not where land is a scarce resource [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. An improved-fallow system in Malawi stayed profitable, with a value-cost ratio above 4.0, only while fertiliser prices were low; when fertiliser prices rose, the comparable rotation fell to a value-cost ratio at or below 2.5 [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. Adoption of improved fallows and biomass transfer in Kenya remained too small in area after six years to produce a significant household-level welfare impact [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are from low- and lower-middle-income countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, with one upper-middle-income harm finding from China.

effect_mechanism: FMNR and related regeneration-based farmland raise rural household income through tree products and diversified livelihoods. In the Sahel, moving from low to continuous Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) practice is associated with an increase in gross household income per capita of about 13%, through sale and own use of fuelwood, fodder, fruit, leaves and other products from the regenerated trees, and moving from low to new/young practice with a 10% increase in gross income through the same pathway [ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_1]. In Niger, FMNR adoption raised gross annual household income by between 22,805 and 27,950 FCFA (46 to 56 USD) per capita, an 18 to 24% increase, with an estimated annual benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 and a 20-year net present value of €772/ha [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Sale of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR is reported to raise income across all social categories, including the very vulnerable [ev_household_income_abasse23_1]; a separate estimate put the annual value of FMNR, through improved soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, at US$56 per hectare in Niger [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7], and the social return on investment of a Ghanaian FMNR project at US$655-887 per household per year [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8]. In Senegal, FMNR-adopting households gained on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber forest products, against 29.73 USD for non-adopters [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In Honduras, farmers using the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system gained a new income stream from renting their land for livestock grazing, because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7]. Across its project countries, a World Vision meta-analysis found participants 15 percentage points more likely than non-participants to report an increase in household income and nine percentage points more likely to report a decrease in community poverty, an effect reported similarly by poorer households, female-headed households and female respondents [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates farm income increased, noting diversified income from wood, honey, medicinal products and other non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income]. A CILSS regional synthesis adds further Sahelian returns. For protecting natural regeneration on farmland in Niger, the internal rate of return was 31 percent, built from an initial investment of about 24 person-days of labour per hectare (1,000 FCFA per day, so 24,000 FCFA to start) against 20 years of wood production and a 5 percent millet and stalk gain in the first 4 years; fodder and soil-fertility benefits were left out of the calculation, so the authors consider the return an underestimate [ev_economic_return_botreij09_28]. On Burkina Faso's Central Plateau, farmer-managed natural regeneration returned an internal rate of 24 percent [ev_economic_return_botreij09_33]. A separate Sahelian estimate puts a Nigerien farmer's wood-sales income from the regeneration at more than 100 000 FCFA of fuelwood and construction wood after 5 years, rising as the regeneration ages [ev_household_income_boton10_8].
conditionality: Against this, the same World Vision multi-country meta-analysis finds Uganda a clear outlier: participant households there were significantly less likely to report income improvements, which the authors attribute partly to participants being poorer households with different income-generation opportunities — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, counted here as measured harm [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. Several Sahel income gains are not statistically significant under the authors' own 5% convention (the 10% and 13% gross-income figures, and the low-to-young tree-product-value gain), though the authors describe them as increases [ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_4]. The Honduran and Ghanaian/Nigerien World Vision figures are grey-literature project self-evaluations or practitioner articles by project-promoter staff, with a positive-bias discount, and the World Vision brief itself states the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African, South Asian and Southeast Asian contexts (Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Senegal, Honduras, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Timor-Leste), in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. effect_mechanism: In shaded coffee and cocoa systems, farm profit depends on whether the extra products and resilience from the shade trees outweigh what is given up in crop yield. A pan-tropical review found shaded coffee and cocoa farms had net returns 23% higher than conventional, sun-grown systems [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1]. In Ghana, moderate-shade cocoa plots had 65% higher value of production than near-full-sun cocoa plots once cocoa, intercrops, fruit, fuelwood and timber are all counted [ev_economic_return_hawkins24_3]. In Costa Rica and Guatemala, modelled long-run returns for low-investment coffee farms were positive under high shade but negative on average under low shade [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. Against this, in Nicaragua a multiple regression found coffee net revenue fell as shade-tree diversity rose [ev_economic_return_hagg17_1]; in Ghana, modelling found Rainforest-Alliance-certified shaded cocoa less profitable than an intensive full-sun monoculture assumed to yield 20% more [ev_economic_return_vaast14_4]; and in Ecuador, net margin per hectare was lower under organic cacao agroforestry (US$1,565) than under technified full-sun cacao (US$2,323) [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1].
conditionality: The gains above come from counting the whole system's products (shade-tree fruit, timber, fuelwood) or from a resilience advantage (the high-shade coffee farms' positive long-run return); the losses come from comparisons against an intensively managed or input-heavy full-sun alternative, where the certification premium or extra yield does not fully offset agroforestry's lower yield of the main crop. Whether shaded perennial systems reduce poverty depends on market access for the secondary products and on what the comparison system assumes.
