effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. Along field boundaries, on Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. A meta-analysis of seven African erosion-control studies (Kenya, Nigeria, Zimbabwe) found agroforestry outperformed controls by a response ratio of 5 for runoff and by 7.2 to 8 for soil loss depending on agro-ecological zone (humid vs semi-arid) [ev_runoff_reduction_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. A separate meta-analysis found infiltration rates 75% higher and runoff 57% lower under agroforestry than crop monoculture (an overall 50% reduction in soil erosion), and separated the erosion-rate response ratio by tree type: 0.29 for non-nitrogen-fixing trees against 0.41 for nitrogen-fixing trees (lower is less erosion), a difference the authors found was not statistically significant [ev_runoff_reduction_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_3]. Agroforestry farmland is reported to be more resilient to heavy rainfall through a 20-50% decrease in runoff and an increase in soil-water infiltration [ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2]. In Argentina, soil erosion and soil exhaustion under yerba mate grown as a monoculture were much lower when the crop was grown with trees in an agroforestry system [ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1]. In Costa Rica, shade trees are described as protecting soil from sheet erosion and conserving fertility through organic-matter inputs [ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11]. In Kenya, a farmer in Isiolo County explained that planting trees in a line prevents soil from being swept away by water [ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. IPCC assessments state in general terms that agroforestry limits soil erosion and helps stabilise soils against desertification, over an estimated extent of about 10 million km2 of land with more than 10% tree cover [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ipccsrccl6_5]. In Mexican coffee, the area affected by landslides significantly increased as vegetation complexity was reduced from forest to shaded monoculture [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2]. In Brazilian coffee, accumulated soil loss under shade was 26% of the loss measured in the unshaded area, and accumulated water loss was 44% of the unshaded area's, over the same rainy season [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1, ev_runoff_reduction_decarvalho21_2]. In Niger, farmers and reviewers describe trees in the regenerated fields protecting against wind, reducing erosion and evaporation, and enriching the soil through litter decomposition and nutrients from livestock sheltering in their shade [ev_erosion_hazard_boton10_6].
conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the cross-family, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as strong reductions, linear boundary plantings as moderate, and regeneration-based farmland and shaded perennial systems as slight. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In China, a field study of windbreak patches found windbreaks reduced average wind-erosion soil loss by 20% compared with open farmland [ev_erosion_hazard_chang21_1]. The Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis breaks its result down by agro-ecological zone rather than giving one pooled number, and both erosion response ratios in it are large enough that, alongside the sub-Saharan meta-analysis already in this row, the same publication-bias caution applies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_3]. Most of these newer units are review or assessment statements rather than site measurements: the IPCC and farmland-resilience statements give no size or site, and the Argentine, Costa Rican and Kenyan farmer statements are a review citation, a Spanish-language case description and a single farmer's perception, not a measured erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_ipccar6ch5_5, ev_runoff_reduction_dobhal24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_montagnini15_1, ev_erosion_hazard_villa20_11, ev_t3_flood_erosion_quandt17_6]. The Chinese windbreak study and the Kenya/Nigeria/Zimbabwe meta-analysis add upper-middle-income and LIC/LMIC evidence respectively, broadly consistent with the row's existing transfer. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. Absolute losses were small in both the shaded and unshaded plots on this farm, so the shaded advantage sits on a very low base, and the comparison is a single-farm case study with no replication or significance test, upper-middle-income Brazilian evidence [ev_erosion_hazard_decarvalho21_1].

effect_mechanism: Trees combined with crops, as alley cropping or contour hedgerow intercropping, protect the soil surface with living plants, litter and mulch and bind it with extended fine roots. A review compiling plot and field studies against sole crops found silvoarable agroforestry cut soil loss by 66% on average and water loss by 43% [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The same Nigerian alley-cropping model also projects soil loss directly: over a 20-year horizon on a sloping field, 2 m-spaced Leucaena alley cropping gives the lowest predicted cumulative soil loss of the systems compared (2.5 t/ha), against 17.8 t/ha for the traditional short-cycle bush fallow it is compared with; 4 m spacing follows at 9.9 t/ha, still below the no-till (14 t/ha) and bush-fallow controls [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_2, ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_3]. On a steep hillslope in Laguna, the Philippines, a randomised trial of contour hedgerows (Desmanthus virgatus) on maize-mungbean alleys found annual soil loss fell step-wise with each added practice: from 124 t/ha/yr under the farmer's up-and-down-slope tillage, to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added, to 3 t/ha/yr once the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues were also spread as mulch, to 0.2 t/ha/yr once zero tillage was added on top of hedgerows and mulch; the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment alone also produced only about half as much annual runoff as the farmer's practice [ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3, ev_runoff_reduction_paningbatan95_4]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a randomised trial intercropping peanut with Choerospondias axillaris trees on a sloping field found mean soil loss per rainfall event fell by 25.3% with younger trees and by 32.0% with older trees compared with mono-cropped peanut [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].
conditionality: The review-based average rests on a single review whose percentages are averages of compiled study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and which gives no country or income-group breakdown [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2]. The newer field and modelled evidence now carries most of the weight in this row and points the same way: in Nigeria, a modelled 2 m alley-cropping system gives the lowest predicted 20-year cumulative soil loss of the systems compared, and in the Philippines, a hillside field trial found soil loss fall from 124 to 40 t/ha/yr once contour hedgerows and contour tillage were added to the farmer's practice, falling further to 3 and then 0.2 t/ha/yr as mulch and zero tillage were added on top [ev_erosion_hazard_ehui90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_1, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_2, ev_erosion_hazard_paningbatan95_3]. The Nigerian erosion figures are modelled, not measured, running a simplified USLE-based erosion model calibrated to plot-level erosion rates from the same research station, and the model's own ranking shows erosion as time-dependent: initial erosion rates are lower under no-till than under the 4 m alley, with the alley only overtaking by the end of the 20-year horizon. The Philippines result is bundled: each successive treatment adds a co-practice (contour tillage, then mulch from the hedgerow trimmings and crop residues, then zero tillage) on top of the hedgerows, so the hedgerow-alone share of the reduction cannot be separated from the tillage and mulch changes that go with it, and even the hedgerow-plus-contour-tillage treatment is still called 'considerable' soil loss by the authors, not yet a tolerable rate. Both the Philippines and Nigeria results sit inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Chinese trial is upper-middle-income evidence. The same Chinese trial found a reversal on runoff: mean runoff per event was higher in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, even though soil loss was lower — the authors attribute the higher runoff to surface seals and crusts forming on the untilled soil under and between the tree rows, while tillage of the peanut area itself raised infiltration there; the engine counts this as measured harm for some adopters [ev_runoff_reduction_wei07_3]. In China, mean soil loss per rainfall event fell with both younger and older intercropped trees against mono-cropped peanut, but mean runoff per event was higher in both tree treatments than in the mono-crop — a reversal the authors attribute to surface seals forming on the untilled soil near the trees rather than to the trees raising runoff generally [ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_1, ev_erosion_hazard_wei07_2].

effect_mechanism: Across World Vision FMNR projects, participants were 10 percent points more likely than non-participants to report a reduction in erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. In Niger, farmers and reviewers describe the regenerated trees protecting against wind, reducing erosion and evaporation, and enriching the soil through litter decomposition and nutrients from livestock sheltering in their shade [ev_erosion_hazard_boton10_6].
conditionality: The World Vision result is a reported perception from a self-evaluation in which the FMNR effect cannot be fully separated from other project activities [ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Honduran landslide result is an earlier observation cited in a working paper, for a slash-and-mulch system under very intense rainfall [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].

effect_mechanism: The measured evidence splits on whether trees add water the system can use or compete with crops for it, and the separator is usually which water measure is used — system water-use efficiency (biomass per unit of water used, which counts the tree's own biomass) versus the crop's own soil moisture. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised millet's rainwater-use efficiency by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and raised the millet/cowpea intercrop's water-use efficiency by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In Malawi, a long-running gliricidia agroforestry trial found system water-use efficiency (total above-ground biomass, including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea, by a wide margin (for example 1.43-1.97 g/kg for gliricidia+maize against 0.15-0.54 g/kg for sole maize) [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system retained 15% more soil water in the driest month than slash-and-burn (23% against 8% humidity), equivalent to about 20 mm of extra rainfall and 20 more days a crop could survive without rain, attributed to better infiltration through soil cover and higher organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry improved both infiltration and soil moisture content compared with controls [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. A continental-scale model finds rainfall dependent on upwind tree cover by 10 to 20%, rising with more tree cover and falling with upwind deforestation [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates water availability increased, attributing it to greater water retention raising groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. A second Malawi reading confirms the recharge-season pattern: available soil water tended to be greater in the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase across two further seasons, attributed to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and further seasonal readings of system water-use efficiency confirm gliricidia-based systems using water more efficiently than sole maize or maize-pigeonpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, which the authors attribute to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. In Ghana and across a ten-country cocoa meta-analysis, shaded cocoa and cocoa agroforestry measured significantly lower soil water than full-sun or monoculture systems, attributed to combined shade-tree and crop transpiration raising water uptake [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat grown with Faidherbia albida, intermediate for sole tree and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture showed no difference [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the Canadian prairies, soil water near an old shelterbelt dropped noticeably in one year, tentatively attributed to uptake by the trees and grasses in the preceding fallow year [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In Mexican coffee, high-shade sites showed smaller day-to-day swings in soil water from evaporation than low-shade sites, a buffering benefit rather than a higher measured moisture level, since shaded sites also gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]; a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water lower on the open field than under trees, though not significant at every position [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The class is set from this balance of measured gains and reversals rather than a pooled sign: the sub-practice rows themselves disagree (regeneration-based farmland reads conflicting on its own, shaded perennial and linear boundary read a slight increase in water stress, while cross-family and planted silvoarable read a benefit), so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. Most of the evidence (Niger, Malawi, Ethiopia, Ghana) sits inside the LIC/LMIC target; the Canadian and German units are high-income temperate evidence outside it [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. A French walnut-alley trial adds a further example of the plough-layer-versus-depth split already seen in this row: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the walnut alleys than in the full-sun control through spring, while at depth (50 cm or more) soil water dynamics were very similar between the two systems, consistent with the trees competing for moisture near the surface while deeper water use is comparable [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This is high-income French evidence, from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target. This Chinese result is upper-middle-income evidence and adds to the depth-dependent drying pattern already described for the African and French trials rather than changing it. Set against this, the same Malaysian trial found alley-cropping with bamboo measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy and gaps leaving the ground exposed to radiation — the wrong alley crop can dry the soil rather than conserve it [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]. In Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth and throughout the monitored period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods, which the authors attribute to canopy interception lowering the rainfall reaching the soil and tree root uptake depleting the deeper layers — a clear case of shade drying the soil rather than conserving its moisture, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. In a New Zealand silvopasture, summer water use and end-of-summer soil moisture were no different from open pasture once the trees were four growing seasons old, as the maturing tree roots came to dominate water use across every system; and after a drier-than-normal winter, deep soil moisture under silvopasture was measured lower than under open lucerne, because the trees' higher winter water use had drawn down deep soil water the low winter rain did not replace — a further measured instance of trees competing with the crop or pasture for water under reduced rainfall [ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_1, ev_soil_moisture_pollock08_2]. None of this new evidence names a drought: the Brazilian site describes a below-average-rainfall month and the New Zealand site a below-normal-rainfall winter, not an extreme event. Malaysia and Brazil are upper-middle income and New Zealand high income, extending the pattern of measured splits in this conflicting-evidence row rather than resolving it.

effect_mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; in a Ghanaian cocoa field, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa resulted in higher water uptake and less soil water than under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].
conditionality: Within low- and lower-middle-income evidence the sides still disagree: the sub-Saharan meta-analysis, the Malawi Gliricidia trial and the Niger Ziziphus trial point to less water stress, while the Faidherbia subsoil depletion in Ethiopia and the cocoa soil-water deficits in the meta-analysis and in Ghana point to more [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. The Niger figures are crop biomass per unit of rainfall, from a trial with the trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and the contrast carries block effects [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. The Makoka units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a soil-moisture measurement, and stays on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa units are crop-specific and do not measure crop water stress directly; the Ghanaian study is a single farm with shade trees of Albizia ferruginea and Antiaris toxicaria [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

effect_mechanism: This upper-middle-income scope row rests on two measured results that point opposite ways. In Chiapas, Mexico, a study of shaded coffee farms found soil water in weighing lysimeters fluctuated far less day-to-day under high and medium shade than under low shade, which the author reads as shade buffering soil-moisture loss through evaporation — though the same shaded sites also gain less water after rain, through canopy interception, so the benefit is a steadier moisture level rather than a wetter one [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean soil water potential drier in the tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut, which the authors attribute to tree-crop competition for water, worse in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].

effect_mechanism: In rainfed cropping the measured evidence points both ways. Trees draw down deeper and dry-season soil water: under Faidherbia albida parkland with wheat in Ethiopia, soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Against this, at Makoka available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]; in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]; and water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.43 against 0.52 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1997/98 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. At Sadore in the Nigerien Sahel, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in millet fields raised the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and without fertilizer, and that of a millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]; and at Makoka the generally comparable distribution of water in the profile [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], and no significant treatment effects in the second season, the second season's October, or December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. The Makoka authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. In France, a walnut-alley trial found a similar depth split: soil water in the plough layer was drier under the trees than the full-sun control through spring, while deep soil-water dynamics were very similar between the two systems [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. In Jiangxi Province, China, a peanut-tree alley-cropping trial found the profile-mean (0-150 cm) soil water potential drier in both tree-intercropped treatments than in mono-cropped peanut or either tree monoculture, consistent with tree-crop competition for water, with the difference larger in the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_wei07_4].
conditionality: What separates the sides is timing and depth: the trees deplete dry-season and subsoil water, so the crop may start the season with less, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. The African studies all involve pruned trees: heavily pruned Faidherbia on farmers' fields, gliricidia pruned before and during the crop season, and Ziziphus pruned before sowing; denser or unpruned canopies are not covered [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]. The water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of trees and crops together per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water, so the tree biomass lifts the tree-system values [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the Niger figures, by contrast, count crop biomass only per mm of rainfall, so they show the crop itself using rain more efficiently with trees nearby [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1]; the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured and the gap is probably overstated, and these units count for water stress only, held out of the production gap because they do not measure crop yield. The German trial counts little: it is a temperate high-income site, its differences were not significant at all positions, and it measured surface soil only [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it measures soil water close to the belt rather than crop water stress, the drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and the authors hedge its cause [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. No study in this cell measures crop water stress itself; soil moisture and water productivity are read as components of it. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The French result is high-income temperate evidence from a single season and site, outside the LIC/LMIC target, and it echoes the same depth-dependent pattern already described for the African trials: near-surface drying under the trees but little difference at depth [ev_soil_moisture_blan22_4, ev_soil_moisture_blan22_5]. This Chinese result is upper-middle-income evidence, adding a further harm reading to the depth-dependent drying pattern already in this row rather than changing it.

effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
conditionality: This row rolls up all tree-perennial farming-system evidence regardless of sub-practice family; in practice all three units come from shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa, coffee). Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. Every other new unit adds to the drying side already dominant in this row: the same Malaysian trial found bamboo alleys measured significantly drier topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to bamboo's sparse canopy leaving the ground exposed [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_2]; and in Brazilian coffee, soil moisture under shade was measured lower than under the unshaded area at every depth throughout the monitoring period, with the drying most pronounced soon after rain in drier periods — shade drying the soil rather than conserving it, even though the authors separately argue tree-coffee water-use complementarity kept available water sufficient for the coffee through the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_5, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_6, ev_soil_moisture_decarvalho21_7]. None of the new units states a size or names a drought, and all are upper-middle-income evidence (Malaysia, Brazil), consistent with this row's existing transfer.

effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control, with a weighted response ratio of 1.6 for soil moisture across 62 observations from 27 studies, and 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1 [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. Wetter soil under trees eases the crop's water stress. A cited statement adds that rainfall over agricultural land can shift with continental land cover, increasing with more upwind tree cover [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4].
conditionality: The meta-analysis pools agroforestry practices without separating soil depth, so it cannot show whether trees and crops compete for deeper water; the Faidherbia parkland evidence that does show subsoil depletion sits in the regeneration-farmland row [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. The effect on infiltration was greater than that on soil moisture [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. On the side of more water stress, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field, while the authors observed no variation in topsoil moisture content between treatments [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. In Malaysian oil palm, alley-cropping with black pepper or cacao measured significantly wetter topsoil than the monocultures, attributed to greater leaf area, lower light penetration and reduced wind cutting evaporation from exposed soil — the one unit in this row's newer evidence that reads as a soil-moisture benefit [ev_soil_moisture_ashraf19_1].
